actions.name: PHQ-9 depression screen
actions.result: PHQ-9 total score = 14/27 (moderate depression). Items endorsed: little interest/pleasure (2), feeling down/depressed (2), sleep trouble (2), fatigue (2), concentration difficulty (3), appetite change (1), feelings of failure/letting family down (2), thoughts of being better off dead or self-harm = 0 (not endorsed). Functional impairment: 'somewhat difficult' to get things done.

actions.name: Columbia-Protocol / suicide risk screen (C-SSRS screener)
actions.result: Denies current or past suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. Denies self-harm history. No access-to-lethal-means concerns elicited. Low acute risk at this time; routine monitoring recommended.

actions.name: GAD-7 anxiety screen
actions.result: GAD-7 total score = 9/21 (mild anxiety), driven mainly by worry about schoolwork and letting family down; no panic attacks reported.

actions.name: Bereavement/grief impact assessment
actions.result: Grandmother (primary caregiver during childhood) died approximately 7 weeks ago per patient report. Patient attended funeral and returned to campus after a brief period to resume academic obligations. Duration of symptoms is under 6 months; functional criteria for prolonged grief disorder are not currently met, though co-occurring depressive symptoms and academic impact warrant monitoring. Pattern consistent with acute grief complicated by academic pressure.

actions.name: Mental status exam (via video)
actions.result: Alert, oriented, cooperative. Speech soft but coherent, normal rate. Mood 'tired, kind of numb.' Affect restricted, occasionally tearful when discussing grandmother. Thought process linear/logical. No evidence of psychosis, mania, or disorganized thinking. Insight and judgment intact.

actions.name: Academic and functional impact assessment
actions.result: Reports missed two assignment deadlines and failed one quiz this semester; placed on academic probation per adviser referral. Attributes difficulty to poor concentration and fatigue rather than lack of understanding of material. Attends most classes but describes 'zoning out.'

actions.name: Social support and disclosure assessment
actions.result: Has not disclosed emotional struggles to family; minimal disclosure to peers. Identifies academic adviser and this counseling referral as current points of contact. Previously active in campus gospel choir (stopped attending ~6 weeks ago) which had been a primary support/coping outlet.

actions.name: Substance use screening
actions.result: Denies alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, or other substance use. No history of substance use treatment.

actions.name: Sleep and appetite review
actions.result: Reports falling asleep without difficulty but waking 2-3 times nightly and feeling unrested; estimates averaging 5-6 hours/night currently versus 7-8 hours baseline before her grandmother's death, based on general recall (no formal sleep log kept). Appetite decreased, skipping breakfast most days; mild unintentional weight change not yet quantified by patient.

actions.name: Review academic adviser referral note
actions.result: Referral note (see d1) documents that the student was placed on academic probation and was referred for counseling as part of the probation support plan, with the adviser noting the student appeared withdrawn and fatigued in a recent meeting.

actions.name: Review prior counseling center contact history
actions.result: No prior contact with university counseling services. This is patient's first behavioral health visit of any kind on record.

actions.name: Review intake demographic and insurance/eligibility form
actions.result: Enrolled full-time, eligible for university counseling services at no additional cost (covered by student health fee). First-generation college student status confirmed on intake form.

actions.name: Readiness/engagement in counseling assessment
actions.result: Patient voices ambivalence about whether 'counseling is for people like us' and concern about confidentiality reaching family; after explanation of confidentiality limits, expresses willingness to try at least 3 sessions to 'see how it goes.'

actions.name: Safety planning discussion (home environment/means)
actions.result: No firearms or stockpiled medications reported in dorm room. No current safety concerns identified; standard crisis line and campus emergency contact information reviewed and provided.

artifacts.title: Intake Assessment / DAP Progress Note (in progress)
artifacts.author: Counseling Trainee (learner)
artifacts.body:
DATA: 19 y/o first-generation nursing student presents for counseling intake following academic adviser referral after placement on academic probation. Reports low mood, poor concentration, sleep and appetite disruption, and withdrawal from a previously valued support activity (gospel choir) since her grandmother's death 7 weeks ago. Grandmother was primary caregiver in childhood. Patient returned to campus 4 days after the funeral to sit exams. Denies SI/HI, denies substance use. Has not disclosed struggles to family; voices belief that family is 'counting on her' and ambivalence about whether counseling is appropriate for her. PHQ-9 14 (moderate), GAD-7 9 (mild). MSE notable for restricted/tearful affect, otherwise unremarkable.

ASSESSMENT: Presentation consistent with Adjustment Disorder with depressed mood / uncomplicated bereavement complicated by academic and financial stressors, acculturative stress as first-generation student, and limited social disclosure of distress. No evidence of prolonged grief disorder at this time (duration <6 months). No acute safety concerns identified.

PLAN: [to be completed by learner]

objectives.text: Conduct a trauma-informed, culturally responsive intake that elicits the grief history, academic stressors, and family/financial context without pathologizing cultural or religious coping.
Screen systematically for suicide risk and safety, and correctly document a low-risk formulation while still providing crisis resources.
Administer and interpret standardized depression and anxiety measures (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and integrate scores with clinical interview data.
Identify and explore the patient's ambivalence about counseling, stigma, and confidentiality concerns related to family, and build engagement rather than confronting these beliefs directly.
Recognize the mismatch between the adviser's documented bereavement timeline and the patient's report, and reconcile discrepancies collaboratively rather than accusingly.

Formulate an appropriate within-scope plan (grief/adjustment-focused counseling, behavioral activation, academic coaching referral) and recognize this case does not require psychiatric referral at this time given denied SI and moderate (not severe) symptom burden.

mismatches.patientClaim: Nia says her grandmother died about 7 weeks ago and she hasn't really talked to anyone at school about it besides the adviser knowing 'a little.'
mismatches.recordEvidence: The adviser's referral note (d1) documents only that the student appeared 'withdrawn and fatigued' in their meeting and recommended counseling as part of the probation plan - it contains no detail about a bereavement, timeline, or emotional disclosure, consistent with the adviser having been told very little.
mismatches.teachingPoint: When a referral source's documentation contains far less detail than what the patient eventually discloses in counseling, this usually reflects guarded or limited disclosure at the time of the earlier contact, not deception; the counselor should recognize this gap as an opportunity to validate how hard it can be to share such things with an adviser, rather than treat it as a credibility problem.

facts.chart: Presents for counseling intake after academic adviser referral following placement on academic probation; reports difficulty concentrating and low mood.
facts.says: My adviser said I should come talk to someone because my grades dropped and I got put on probation. I guess I've been having a hard time focusing.

facts.chart: Grandmother, who raised patient, died approximately 7 weeks ago; patient returned to campus 4 days after the funeral to take exams.
facts.says: My grandma passed about seven weeks ago. She's the one who really raised me. I only stayed home four days before I had to come back for exams.

facts.chart: Reports significant difficulty concentrating in class and while studying, describes 'zoning out.'
facts.says: I'll be sitting in class and realize I haven't heard anything the professor said in ten minutes. It's like my brain just checks out.

facts.chart: Reports frequent unexpected crying episodes, often in library restroom, several times per week.
facts.says: I end up crying in the bathroom stalls in the library sometimes. I don't even always know what sets it off.

facts.chart: Reports fragmented sleep, waking multiple times nightly, averaging 5-6 hours versus baseline 7-8 hours.
facts.says: I fall asleep okay but then I'm up at like 2 or 3 am and can't really get back to sleep right. I'm tired all the time now.

facts.chart: Stopped attending campus gospel choir approximately 6 weeks ago; previously described as a main source of comfort and community.
facts.says: I used to go to gospel choir every week, it was my favorite thing honestly. I haven't gone since I got back from the funeral. I just don't have it in me.

facts.chart: Works approximately 25 hours/week at campus dining hall in addition to full course load.
facts.says: I work at the dining hall, like 25 hours a week some weeks, to help send money home and cover my own stuff.

facts.chart: Sends a portion of earnings home to support family; feels financial responsibility toward them.
facts.says: I send some of my paycheck back home when I can. My mama's got a lot on her plate.

facts.chart: Reports strong sense that family is 'counting on her' to succeed as the first in the family to attend college; associated guilt and pressure.
facts.says: Everybody back home is counting on me. I'm the first one in my family to even go to college, let alone nursing school. I can't let them down.

facts.chart: Denies current or past suicidal ideation, intent, plan, or self-harm.
facts.says: No, I would never do anything like that. I just feel sad and tired, not like I want to hurt myself.

facts.chart: Denies access concerns; no firearms or stockpiled medication in residence.
facts.says: I don't have anything like that in my dorm room, no.

facts.chart: Reports decreased appetite, frequently skipping breakfast; has not weighed herself recently.
facts.says: I just don't feel hungry in the mornings anymore. I used to eat breakfast every day, now I skip it most of the time.

facts.chart: No known family history of diagnosed mental illness; grandmother sometimes described as 'the strong one' who 'didn't believe in dwelling on things.'
facts.says: Nobody in my family really talks about stuff like depression. My grandma used to say you just pray on it and keep moving.

facts.chart: Reports feeling out of place academically and socially compared to classmates whose parents are physicians or other professionals.
facts.says: A lot of the girls in my program, their parents are doctors or whatever. They talk about stuff like it's nothing, and I feel like I'm always behind.

facts.chart: Reports missing two assignment deadlines and failing one quiz this semester, contributing to probation.
facts.says: I missed two assignments and bombed a quiz. That's basically why I got put on probation.

facts.chart: Describes roommate relationship as 'fine, we just don't talk much'; no conflict reported. (Distractor - not primary driver of symptoms.)
facts.says: My roommate's okay, we just kind of keep to ourselves. We're not close but it's not bad or anything.

facts.chart: Reports a brief cold/sinus congestion about 3 weeks ago, self-resolved, unrelated to current presenting concerns. (Distractor.)
facts.says: Oh, I did have a cold a few weeks back, stuffy nose for like a week, but that cleared up on its own.

facts.chart: Denies alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, or other substance use.
facts.says: No, I don't drink or smoke or anything like that.

facts.chart: No prior mental health treatment or counseling history before this intake.
facts.says: I've never talked to a counselor before, this is my first time.

facts.chart: Reports telling adviser only limited information about the bereavement, without full detail about ongoing symptoms.
facts.says: I told my adviser a little bit about my grandma passing when she asked why I seemed off, but I didn't really get into everything else.

facts.chart: Describes faith/church community as historically important coping resource but currently feels disconnected from it since grandmother's death.
facts.says: Church and choir used to be where I felt closest to God and to her. Now I don't even want to go, it just makes me think of her more.

facts.chart: Expresses ambivalence about whether counseling is appropriate for 'people like us,' citing lack of family familiarity with therapy.
facts.says: Honestly, I don't know if counseling is really a thing for people like us. Nobody in my family's ever done anything like this.

facts.chart: Worries that information shared in counseling could get back to her family and worsen their worry or disapproval.
facts.says: I don't want any of this getting back to my mama. She's got enough to worry about, and I don't want her thinking I can't handle things.

facts.chart: Patient appears to test whether counselor is genuinely listening, sometimes pausing to see if details are reflected back accurately.
facts.says: [after sharing something] ...did that make sense, or are you just writing stuff down?

facts.chart: States primary goal is to 'get back on track' academically and stop crying unexpectedly; secondary interest in processing grief if trust is established.
facts.says: I guess I just want to stop falling apart in random places and get my grades back up. Maybe talk about my grandma too, if that's what this is for.

facts.chart: Relies on dining hall shifts for most meals; reports eating adequately at lunch/dinner despite skipping breakfast.
facts.says: I eat okay at lunch and dinner since I work at the dining hall, it's really just breakfast I skip now.

facts.chart: Reports loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (choir, texting friends back home) and low energy most of the day.
facts.says: I don't really feel like doing anything anymore, even texting my friends back home. I'm just tired, all day, every day.

facts.chart: Has two younger siblings at home who look up to her as a role model for going to college.
facts.says: I've got two little brothers back home, and they kind of look up to me for being the one who made it to college.

facts.chart: Feels guilty for 'not grieving properly' and for returning to campus so soon after the funeral instead of staying longer with family.
facts.says: I feel bad that I didn't stay home longer. Like I didn't even really grieve right before I had to come back and act normal for exams.

facts.chart: Lives in a shared dormitory room on campus; no reported housing instability.
facts.says: I live in the dorms with my roommate, that part's fine.

patient.name: Nia Thompson
patient.occupation: Full-time nursing student; part-time dining hall worker
patient.appearance: A young woman with box braids pulled back, wearing a campus dining-hall polo as if on a break between shifts. She sits on the edge of her dorm bed with a textbook visible on the desk behind her; the lighting is dim and the room is tidy but sparse. Her posture is slightly hunched, eyes often lowered, with a polite, careful expression that occasionally cracks into tearfulness before she composes herself again.

persona.personality: Soft-spoken, polite, conscientious, and guarded; carries herself with quiet dignity and a strong sense of duty to family.
persona.communicationStyle: Measured and respectful, often pausing before answering sensitive questions; may test whether the counselor is truly listening before disclosing more. Minimizes her own distress initially ('I'm fine, really').
persona.emotionalState: Fatigued, subdued, intermittently tearful when discussing her grandmother; anxious about being judged and about counseling getting back to her family.
persona.background: Grew up in a small rural town in Mississippi, raised primarily by her grandmother alongside her mother and two younger brothers. First in her family to attend college; chose nursing partly to honor her grandmother, who had wanted to be a nurse but could not afford it. Active for years in her home church choir and continued in a campus gospel choir until recently. Works dining hall shifts to cover personal expenses and send money home.
speechExamples: I don't want to make a big deal out of it, everybody's got problems.
My grandma used to say the Lord doesn't put more on you than you can bear, so I feel like I should be able to handle this.
I guess I just didn't expect it to still be this hard, seven weeks out.
Is it okay if what I say here doesn't get back to my mama somehow?
...did that make sense, or are you just writing stuff down?
concerns: Whether counseling will actually help or is 'not for people like her'
Confidentiality - fear that family will find out she is struggling
Falling further behind academically and losing her nursing program standing
Guilt about not grieving her grandmother 'the right way'
Letting her family and younger siblings down after being the first to attend college

scenario.studentBrief: You are a counseling trainee at a university counseling center conducting a telehealth intake session with Nia Thompson, a 19-year-old first-generation nursing student referred by her academic adviser after being placed on academic probation. Review the referral note before the session. Conduct a trauma-informed intake, screen for risk, and begin a collaborative plan.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Difficulty concentrating and declining academic performance following the death of her grandmother seven weeks ago; referred by academic adviser after being placed on academic probation.
scenario.openingLine: Hi, I'm Nia. My adviser said I should talk to someone because my grades slipped and I got put on probation. I guess I've just been having a hard time focusing lately.
tasks: Build rapport and conduct a culturally responsive intake exploring presenting concerns, academic stress, and support system
Administer and interpret the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, and complete a suicide risk screen
Explore the patient's understanding of counseling and address any questions or concerns about the process
Review available documentation and clarify any questions about the referral
Draft the Assessment and Plan sections of a DAP note reflecting an appropriate within-scope plan

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in her university dormitory room
profile.summary: A 19-year-old first-generation nursing student presents for a counseling intake after academic probation, seven weeks after the death of the grandmother who raised her. The case teaches culturally responsive grief and adjustment counseling, systematic risk screening with standardized measures, and recognizing when a presentation remains within counseling scope (no psychiatric referral needed) versus requiring escalation.
profile.title: Academic Probation and Recent Bereavement in a First-Generation Nursing Student

answerKey.primaryProblem: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood / acute grief reaction (uncomplicated bereavement at 7 weeks) complicated by academic stress, financial responsibility, and acculturative/first-generation stress
differential: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (most consistent given clear precipitant, 7-week timeline, and functional impact)
Major depressive episode (consider given PHQ-9=14 and anhedonia/sleep/appetite changes; monitor if symptoms persist or worsen beyond expected adjustment course)
Normal/uncomplicated grief reaction (expected sadness, crying, longing within first weeks-months after loss of a primary attachment figure)
Prolonged grief disorder - not met at this time (requires ~6+ months duration); flag for reassessment if symptoms persist
Generalized anxiety (mild, per GAD-7=9, secondary to academic/financial pressures) rather than a primary anxiety disorder
keyFindings: Denies current/past suicidal ideation, intent, plan, or self-harm; no access-to-means concerns
Grandmother (primary attachment figure) died 7 weeks ago; patient returned to campus after only 4 days to take exams
Withdrawal from gospel choir, a primary coping/support outlet, since the loss
Significant guilt about family financial dependence, probation status, and 'not grieving properly' (disclosed only with rapport, not volunteered automatically)
Ambivalence about counseling and fear that disclosures will reach family, reflecting stigma and confidentiality concerns rather than lack of need

The adviser's referral note documents far less detail about the bereavement than the patient ultimately shares in session, reflecting limited disclosure at the time of the adviser meeting rather than inconsistency in the patient's story
plan: Continue weekly individual counseling focused on grief processing and adjustment to loss, paced to patient's readiness and cultural/spiritual framework
Use behavioral activation to re-engage with previously valued coping activities (e.g., gradual return to choir or faith community) as tolerated, not as an assignment imposed on her
Collaboratively discuss confidentiality parameters and limits early, directly addressing her fear that sessions could 'get back' to her family

Reassess PHQ-9/GAD-7 and suicide risk at each session; no current indication for psychiatric referral or higher level of care given denied SI and moderate (not severe) symptom range, but escalate immediately if risk changes
Coordinate (with patient's consent) with academic adviser regarding academic coaching/support resources tied to the probation plan; avoid disclosing clinical content without explicit consent
Provide psychoeducation normalizing grief trajectory and gently distinguish expected grief from clinical depression, revisiting if symptoms persist beyond ~6 months or significantly worsen
Explore financial stress and work hours (25 hrs/week) as a contributing stressor; consider referral to campus financial aid/work-study resources if patient is interested
Document DAP note capturing data, adjustment/grief-focused assessment, and plan above; flag case for routine (not urgent) supervisor review given first intake
redFlags: Any emergence of suicidal ideation, hopelessness escalation, or access to lethal means - would require immediate safety planning and possible escalation beyond counseling scope
Symptoms persisting or worsening despite counseling and behavioral activation over several weeks - consider referral for psychiatric medication evaluation
Signs of prolonged grief disorder criteria being met at the 6-month mark (intense yearning, identity disruption, inability to engage in activities)
Significant further academic/functional decline suggesting need for more intensive support (e.g., medical leave, higher level of care)
educationPoints: Grief at 7 weeks after losing a primary caregiver, including crying spells, sleep/appetite change, and reduced interest, is within the range of expected acute bereavement and should not be immediately pathologized as a disorder
Standardized screens (PHQ-9, GAD-7, suicide risk screen) should be interpreted alongside context (recent loss, academic/financial stress) rather than in isolation
Cultural and faith-based coping (prayer, 'the Lord doesn't put more on you than you can bear') should be respected as a resource, not treated as denial or avoidance to be corrected

Stigma and unfamiliarity with counseling in first-generation students/families is a common and valid barrier to engagement, best addressed through transparency about confidentiality and collaborative goal-setting rather than persuasion

Sensitive material such as guilt about grief timing or ambivalence about counseling often only emerges once trust is established - a structured screen or referral note cannot substitute for a rapport-building interview

Minor discrepancies between a referral source's note and the patient's own account often reflect differing depth of disclosure at different times, not deception - clarify gently and non-confrontationally

Recognizing the limits of counseling scope (no diagnosis of a chronic psychiatric disorder requiring medication, no prescribing) and knowing when routine monitoring is appropriate versus when referral/escalation is needed is a core competency
